title: Evaluating Explainability: A Framework for Systematic Assessment of Explainable AI Features in Medical Imaging
key_finding: Authors from the US FDA device centre propose a staged framework for testing heatmap-type explanations of imaging AI on four criteria: consistency (stability under small input changes, scored with SSIM, MSE or IoU), plausibility (overlap with lesion ground truth), fidelity (model-parameter randomisation and incremental deletion) and usefulness (human reader studies), plus an 'explainability card' for reporting. In a case study with 150 synthetic mammograms (M-SYNTH) and a Faster R-CNN detector, Ablation-CAM scored higher than Eigen-CAM on plausibility and fidelity, while both maps fluctuated under dose and rotation changes that left detection accuracy stable. Usefulness was not tested, no acceptance thresholds are set, and exact metric values are given only in figures.
use_for: 1 - regulator-authored framework naming the four evaluation axes (consistency, plausibility, fidelity, usefulness) and a reporting card; supports the argument that faithfulness and plausibility must be tested separately and before reader studies
verified_how: MDPI article page (abstract and full text read)
flags: Case study uses synthetic mammography only, not chest CT. Numeric results appear only in figures, so no headline number is recorded. Affiliations are given for the group as a whole on the page.

title: Evaluating the robustness of explainable AI in medical image recognition under natural and adversarial data corruption
key_finding: Benchmarks the stability of ten post-hoc explanation methods (eight for CNNs including Integrated Gradients, SmoothGrad, Grad-CAM and Grad-CAM++; AttnLRP and LibraGrad for transformers) on eight classifiers across three MedMNIST sets (dermatoscopy, paediatric chest radiographs with 5,856 images, retinal OCT), under natural corruptions (contrast reduction, JPEG compression, speckle noise) and an adversarial attack that alters the explanation while keeping the predicted class. Stability is scored with L2 distance, SSIM and a new spatial metric (Convolution Density Agreement); 160 configurations per data set. Many methods changed under imperceptible perturbations and no method was best on every metric: SmoothGrad was most stable against the attack and Grad-CAM++ against natural noise for CNNs.
use_for: 1 (also 2) - robustness/stability of saliency maps as a separate evaluation axis, with a head-to-head comparison of ten attribution methods that includes chest radiographs
verified_how: Springer article page (abstract and full text read) + Crossref record for the author list
flags: Springer page truncates the byline with an ellipsis; the six-author list is taken from Crossref. Table values were not visible in the fetched page, so no numeric scores are quoted. Images are 224x224 MedMNIST benchmarks, not clinical-resolution CT.

title: More than just a heatmap: elevating XAI with rigorous evaluation metrics
key_finding: Introduces XAlign, a single composite score for how well a saliency map matches expert tumour annotations, built from three terms: concentration of attribution inside the lesion, adherence to the lesion boundary, and a penalty for scattered attribution. It is applied to compare Grad-CAM, LIME, SHAP and the native saliency of the authors' own CNN-spiking hybrid classifier (SpikeNet) on TCGA-LGG brain MRI (22-fold patient-level cross-validation) and BUSI breast ultrasound (5-fold); the native maps scored highest on both data sets. The component weights were fixed on a held-out dermoscopy set (ISIC 2019) and not tuned per data set.
use_for: 1 (also 2) - example of a composite/unified explanation-quality index (plausibility type, mask based) and of post-hoc methods being ranked head-to-head on MRI
verified_how: Frontiers article page (abstract and full text read)
flags: The metric is proposed together with the authors' own model, which it ranks first, so the comparison is not independent. Several result tables rendered blank in the fetched page, so no XAlign values are quoted. XAlign measures agreement with annotations (plausibility), not faithfulness. Page gives a publication date of 28 October 2025 and an earlier online date of 9 October 2025 in its metadata.

title: XIMED: A Dual-Loop Evaluation Framework Integrating Predictive Model and Human-Centered Approaches for Explainable AI in Medical Imaging
key_finding: Proposes a two-part evaluation of explanation methods for chest radiograph classification and applies it to LIME and SHAP. The model-centred loop checks whether explanations respond as expected to changes in model inputs, outputs and internal structure; the human-centred loop is a study with 97 medical experts who rated trust, confidence and agreement with supporting and opposing evidence before and after seeing explanations. Both methods reacted to model changes; SHAP had more influence on diagnostic changes and helped correct wrong initial diagnoses, and explanations raised trust and agreement when the clinician's first diagnosis was correct.
use_for: 1 (also 3) - framework that couples computational checks with a human study; evidence that LIME and SHAP differ in their effect on clinicians reading chest radiographs
flags: Only the abstract was summarised; the data set name, classifier and effect sizes are not stated there and are not recorded. Experts are described as 'medical experts', not specifically radiologists.

title: Attention Without Grounding: Causal Evaluation of Visual Explanations in Medical VLMs
key_finding: Audits heatmap explanations of chest radiograph vision-language models (three MedGemma-4B variants, LLaVA-RAD, Qwen3-VL, CheXagent) on three axes: overlap with radiologist boxes on PadChest (n=637), pointing game, attribution mass in mask and pixel-AP against radiologist masks on CheXlocalize (n=643), and patch-occlusion causal maps with insertion/deletion curves. Six attribution methods are compared (raw attention, attention rollout, gradient x attention, Winsor-CAM, integrated gradients, RISE). No vision-language model passed: none placed more than 22% of attribution inside the radiologist mask and attention was negatively correlated with causal importance (Spearman rho -0.05 to -0.17), whereas Grad-CAM on two chest-radiograph CNN classifiers passed the same protocol (p<1e-4 versus shuffled maps).
use_for: 2 - head-to-head failure of several attribution methods on chest radiographs using localisation and causal (deletion/insertion, occlusion) metrics together; shows that plausible-looking maps from vision-language models are not faithful
flags: PREPRINT, not peer reviewed; no venue stated in the text read (formatted like a conference submission). Chest radiographs, not CT. First posted 2026-07-20 according to alphaXiv; version read is v2 dated 11 Aug 2026. Authors report using an LLM for language editing. No published version found by web search on 2026-10-10.

title: Faithful Faithfulness Evaluations: Challenges & Pitfalls Learned from a Breast MRI Case Study
key_finding: Compares seven saliency methods (last-layer attention, attention rollout, Grad-SAM, gradient attention rollout, GMAR, Grad-CAM, HiResCAM) for a transformer classifier of 3D breast MRI (ODELIA challenge data, 1,022 unilateral breast volumes, 116 in the test set) using deletion and insertion curves summarised as area under the confidence curve. Method rankings changed with the masking strategy (black, white, minimum intensity, attention masking); with fixed-intensity masking most methods were close to random ordering. Grad-CAM and gradient attention rollout were the strongest class-specific methods (deletion AUCC 0.336 each versus 0.512 for random), but their order depended on the protocol, and the advantage shrank when class-agnostic variants were compared.
use_for: 2 (also 1) - disagreement between saliency methods on volumetric MRI and the dependence of deletion/insertion rankings on how regions are removed; caution for any faithfulness table reported in chest CT studies
flags: PREPRINT, not peer reviewed; no venue stated. Breast MRI, single model with moderate accuracy (macro AUROC 0.73). The classifier processes volumes slice-wise. No published version found by web search on 2026-10-10.

title: Decision processes in 3D structural MRI schizophrenia classification evaluated with saliency maps
key_finding: Trained seven 3D deep learning architectures (two from scratch, five pretrained) to separate schizophrenia from controls on T1-weighted MRI of 192 adults (101 patients, 91 controls; MCIC collection) and examined each with Grad-CAM. Plausibility was judged visually and with two quantitative measures: share of saliency mass inside the brain, and centre-of-mass deviation and spread. All models reached similar accuracy (above 70%, AUC above 0.75, no significant differences), yet only two of the seven (BrainID and ResNet18) based their decisions on plausible brain structure.
use_for: 2 (also 4) - volumetric example where equal accuracy hides different decision bases: saliency maps exposed five of seven 3D models as relying on implausible regions
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract and full text read)
flags: Brain MRI, not chest imaging. Only Grad-CAM was used, so this compares models rather than explanation methods. Small single-collection sample without lesion-level ground truth.

title: Evaluating cognitive biases in AI-assisted mammography interpretation: a simulation reader study of explainable AI across radiologist experience levels
key_finding: Single-centre, fully crossed simulation study: six breast radiologists of three experience levels read 200 mammograms unaided, with AI, and with AI plus saliency heatmaps; the AI's BI-RADS-like recommendation was deliberately shifted by one category in 30% of examinations. Without heatmaps, automation bias occurred in 65/180 (36.1%) and anchoring-related revision in 61/180 (33.9%) manipulated readings; with heatmaps these fell to 32/180 (17.8%) and 31/180 (17.2%) (adjusted odds ratios 0.56 and 0.61, both p<0.001). On unmanipulated cases accuracy rose from 86.2% unaided to 90.1% with AI plus heatmaps; less experienced readers were most affected and the bias was reduced but not removed.
use_for: 3 - experimental evidence that heatmap explanations can roughly halve, but not eliminate, automation and anchoring bias when the AI is wrong
flags: Mammography, six readers, one centre, enriched case mix and an artificially high AI error rate. The 180-reading denominator per condition is as reported in the abstract and was not reconciled with 200 cases x 6 readers x 30% from the full text.

title: Automation Bias in Action: Eye Tracking of Humans Reading Screening Mammograms with and without AI Prompts
key_finding: Retrospective paired multireader study with eye tracking: 10 readers from the UK breast screening programme read 60 two-view screening mammograms unaided and, six weeks later, with a commercial AI tool that displayed region prompts (26 true-positive, 14 false-negative, 14 false-positive, 6 true-negative AI outputs). For cancers the AI missed, median reader sensitivity fell from 71% unaided to 39% with AI (P=.002); for false-positive AI cases median specificity rose from 21% to 39% (P=.004). Reading time rose with the number of prompts (median 25 s with none to 34 s with four or more) and fixation rate on missed cancers was lower with AI.
use_for: 3 - direct measurement of automation bias and altered visual search from incorrect localisation prompts; reading-time cost of on-image AI marks
flags: Mammography; the 'explanation' here is a localisation prompt with a score, not a saliency map. Article e-number not shown on the page (pages left null). Study funded by the AI vendor (Lunit), stated as not involved in the article.

title: The impact of AI feedback on the accuracy of diagnosis, decision switching and trust in radiography
key_finding: Online experiment with 94 participants (54 student and 40 qualified radiographers) who each judged three upper-limb radiographic examinations before AI feedback, after a Grad-CAM-style heatmap, and after a binary AI diagnosis with a percentage confidence. The ResNet-152 model was correct on only 12 of the 21 examinations used. Feedback improved accuracy when the AI was right but accuracy fell when it was wrong (by 9.6% for students and 4.3% for radiographers); in abnormal cases the heatmap alone lowered accuracy (65.85% to 57.62%) before the binary output raised it to 72.35%. Students switched decisions more often than radiographers (23.5% vs 14.3% after the heatmap) and self-reported trust dropped by 0.7 points on a 5-point scale in both groups.
use_for: 3 - comparison of two feedback forms (heatmap versus label with confidence) on accuracy, decision switching and trust; shows a heatmap alone can mislead less experienced readers
verified_how: PLOS ONE article page (abstract and full text read) + Ulster University repository record
flags: Readers are radiographers and students, not radiologists; musculoskeletal radiographs; convenience sample; each participant saw only three examinations. Sixth author is spelled 'Devinder Kumar' on the journal page and 'Deviner Kumar' in the repository record; the journal spelling is used.

title: Eye-Tracking Evidence That Verifiable Explanations Support Visual Evidence Checking in AI-Assisted Chest Radiograph Interpretation
key_finding: A 2x2 between-subjects eye-tracking experiment (verifiable explanation present or absent; high or low risk context) with 56 clinically trained participants (clerkship students, residents, attending physicians; 14 per cell), each completing 24 pleural-effusion decisions on chest radiographs with AI advice that was wrong in 6 trials. Outcomes were gaze switches between the AI output and the image and dwell time on the image. Explanations did not simply raise acceptance: when the AI was wrong, participants with explanations switched between AI output and image more often (about 8.5 vs 6.0 per trial) and looked at the image longer (about 5.1 s vs 4.3 s).
use_for: 3 - process-level (gaze) evidence that explanations which can be checked against the image promote verification of wrong AI advice on chest radiographs
verified_how: MDPI article page (abstract and most of the full text read)
flags: Small cells (14 per condition), mixed training levels, one binary task with fixed case-correctness pairing. Authors present the gaze measures as markers of checking, not proof of better diagnosis. Chest radiographs, not CT.

title: Dermatologist-like explainable AI enhances melanoma diagnosis accuracy: eye-tracking study
key_finding: Reader study with eye tracking in which 76 dermatologists each diagnosed 16 dermoscopic images of melanomas and naevi, first with a plain AI prediction and then with an explainable AI giving domain-specific explanations. Mean balanced accuracy rose from 79.9% with AI to 82.7% with explainable AI (gain 2.8 percentage points, P=0.013). Disagreement with the classifier and difficult lesions were associated with more fixations, read by the authors as higher cognitive load; the accuracy gain was unrelated to years of experience and trust was not measured in this study.
use_for: 3 - non-radiology comparator showing a small but significant accuracy gain from concept-style explanations over AI alone, with gaze data on cognitive load
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract and results read) + Crossref record for the author list
flags: Dermoscopy, not radiology. Byline has 20 named authors, the Reader Study Consortium and the senior author; Crossref also lists about 80 consortium members as individual authors, which are not reproduced here. Fixed order (AI first, then explainable AI) rather than randomised arms; the gain was significant in the webcam cohort (n=51) but not in the device-based cohort (n=25).

title: Exploring Radiologists' Expectations of Explainable Machine Learning Models in Medical Image Analysis
url_opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11700 ; https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2604.11700 (PDF text read through alphaXiv)
key_finding: A 30-question structured survey of 46 respondents (26 radiologists and 20 radiology residents) from the hospitals of one university, most working with CT and MRI. Explainability was called a prerequisite for trust by 42 of 46. The elements most often named as making a model explainable were reliance on clinically relevant imaging features (residents 70%, senior radiologists 86%) and visual heatmaps (65% and 79%); 86% of senior radiologists but no residents wanted standardised radiological scoring systems, and counterfactual explanations were least selected (33%). When model and reader disagree most would examine the explanation before deciding; respondents ranked task performance, then model confidence, then explanation quality when judging outputs, and 78% and 74% asked for external and prospective validation.
use_for: 3 - survey evidence on what radiologists say they want from explanations (relevant features, heatmaps, scoring-system terms, confidence) and how wishes differ by seniority
verified_how: arXiv abstract page + alphaXiv full text of arXiv:2604.11700v1
flags: PREPRINT, not peer reviewed (text says data will be released on acceptance). Single-institution convenience sample; stated preferences, not measured performance. Ethics approval details withheld in the preprint. No published version found by web search on 2026-10-10.

title: Mask of Truth: Model Sensitivity to Unexpected Regions of Medical Images
journal: Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine
key_finding: Tests for shortcut learning by training DenseNet-121 classifiers on chest radiographs with the lungs removed or kept (PadChest, 93,203 images after filtering, five findings; external test on 22,004 ChestX-ray14 images) and on fundus images (Chaksu). Chest models stayed well above chance with the lungs masked out by a bounding box (effusion AUC 0.85-0.93, pneumonia at least 0.74) and above metadata-only baselines, while lung-only images gave AUCs near 0.5 for several findings. SHAP maps pointed to a pacemaker for cardiomegaly and to peripheral image areas; a radiology resident identified only 2 of 35 present conditions on the masked images, and external performance was far lower than internal.
use_for: 4 - masking experiment plus SHAP showing chest radiograph classifiers can perform without the clinically relevant region; also notes that local attribution maps can miss global shortcuts
verified_how: Springer article page (abstract and full text read) + Crossref record
flags: Chest radiographs and fundus, not CT. Online first 20 May 2025; assigned to volume 39 issue 1 (February 2026). Springer page truncated the byline; the five-author list is from Crossref. Crossref short title is recorded as shown.

title: Explainable AI reveals Clever Hans effects in unsupervised learning models
key_finding: Uses explanation methods to show that unsupervised representation-learning and anomaly-detection models, including foundation models, often predict correctly for the wrong reasons. In the medical example a COVID-19 detector built on PubMedCLIP features (2,597 NIH CXR8 radiographs plus 535 images from a public COVID-19 collection) reached 87.5% class-balanced accuracy overall but only 81.7% with a 51% false-positive rate on the COVID-source subset; BiLRP explanations traced this to text-like annotations on the images. The authors attribute the effect largely to inductive biases of the unsupervised learner and report that targeted mitigation improved robustness.
use_for: 4 - Clever Hans effect inherited from a pretrained medical foundation model and exposed by explanations in a chest radiograph task; relevant to foundation-model-based chest CT pipelines
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract and results read) + Crossref record for the author list
flags: The chest radiograph experiment is one of several use cases; most of the paper is general machine learning. Chest radiographs, not CT.

title: Uncertainty-Driven Training for Three-Dimensional Calibrated Lung Nodule Classification
journal: Artificial Neural Networks and Machine Learning - ICANN 2026 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 17092)
key_finding: Proposes a training scheme for 3D CT lung nodule classifiers in which validation-set uncertainty estimates reweight the loss towards unreliable classes, comparing Monte Carlo dropout with evidential deep learning on five backbones (ResNet, DenseNet, EfficientNet, ViT, Swin) using LIDC-IDRI and NoduleMNIST3D. Classification performance stayed similar to standard training while expected calibration error fell by up to 65% on LIDC-IDRI; gains were more consistent for convolutional than transformer backbones, evidential learning degraded on ViT, and simple post-hoc temperature scaling was highly effective in every configuration.
use_for: 5 - chest CT evidence that nodule classifiers are miscalibrated by default and that calibration (expected calibration error) should be reported alongside accuracy; temperature scaling as a strong baseline
verified_how: Springer chapter page (abstract; full text behind preview) + arXiv abstract page 2609.20905
flags: Conference paper (ICANN 2026). Springer shows first online 14 September 2026 but a 2027 copyright/citation year; year is recorded as 2027 with the 2026 online date, so it counts as 2026 under the online-first rule. Only the abstract was read, which gives a single number (up to 65% ECE reduction); absolute ECE values and nodule counts are not recorded. No explanation method or reader study is involved.

title: Human-AI Collaboration in Radiology: The Blind Spots
key_finding: Special report (narrative synthesis, no new data) arguing that radiology AI research has concentrated on stand-alone algorithm performance while the human-AI interaction that determines clinical value is poorly understood. It sets out three under-recognised determinants: cognitive psychology (automation bias, how AI uncertainty is framed, AI-induced skill decay), interface and user-experience design (timing, prominence and documentation of AI findings), and algorithmic conformity driven by medicolegal, transparency and organisational pressure; research directions are proposed for each.
use_for: 5 (also 3) - peer-reviewed synthesis linking how AI output and uncertainty are presented to automation bias and reliance; frames explanation and confidence display as interface-design questions
verified_how: RSNA article page (abstract read; full text paywalled)
flags: Narrative special report, not a systematic review; only the abstract was read. Article e-number not shown on the page (pages left null). Not specific to chest CT.

title: Explainability and AI Confidence in Clinical Decision Support Systems: Effects on Trust, Diagnostic Performance, and Cognitive Load in Breast Cancer Care
key_finding: Web-based interrupted time-series experiment with 28 US clinicians (about 60% radiologists) who diagnosed breast ultrasound images under five successive conditions: no AI, AI label, label with class probabilities, added tumour localisation, and localisation with high- and low-confidence regions (10 images per condition; AI accuracy 81%). In the preprint analysis, low AI confidence lowered trust and agreement and lengthened decisions, whereas high confidence was associated with a small but significant drop in diagnostic performance, interpreted as over-reliance; adding localisation with probabilities significantly increased reported stress, and mental demand did not change significantly.
use_for: 5 (also 3) - evidence that displaying AI confidence changes reliance in both directions: low confidence prompts caution, high confidence invites over-reliance
verified_how: Crossref record (bibliographic data) + Stevens Institute repository record (abstract) + arXiv preprint 2501.16693 read through alphaXiv (methods and results)
flags: Publisher page (tandfonline) could not be opened; the journal abstract was read on the institutional repository page and details come from the arXiv version via an alphaXiv machine-generated report, so numbers may differ from the final article. The repository abstract says high confidence raised trust, while the preprint report gives that effect as not significant. Breast ultrasound, 28 participants, no control arm, condition order not randomised. Crossref prints the journal name with an en dash.
